segment_name: A Society of One's Own: Reading Gissing's Opening World

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these characters are basically *auditioning* their philosophies — performing who they want to be. I want to start there, because that framing feels like it could unlock the whole novel. When Virginia gets that quarter-hour of happiness in Trafalgar Square — that 'delightful animation, rarest of boons' — is she performing too? Or is that the one moment in the opening where someone actually *stops* performing?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan's performance thesis on the table early and immediately test it against its hardest case — Virginia's most intimate moment — to provoke the others

questions.question: Daniel, I have to put this to you directly, because you've said something that I think will drive Edmund slightly mad. You're arguing that Virginia's moment of peace in Trafalgar Square is actually the system being clever — giving her just enough relief that she doesn't cause trouble. Edmund, I suspect, thinks that's a rather cold way to read what Gissing's doing there. So Daniel — make the case. Why is that quarter-hour of 'rarest of boons' not a moment of grace but a kind of trap?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to articulate the structural reading at its sharpest, setting up direct collision with Leigh's spiritual reading of the same passage

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Everard's free union declaration — 'My companion must be as independent of forms as I am myself' — you've called it *ice*. You hear a man describing his own capacity for abandonment. But Daniel would say the problem with Everard isn't his coldness, it's his blindness — he's dismantling the wrong forms entirely. Who's got the better reading? And does it matter which one Gissing intended?
questions.intent: Get Leigh's moral reading of Everard into direct conversation with Rosen's structural critique — two very different ways of condemning the same character

questions.question: Let's go to Mary's big speech — where she declares herself 'a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person.' Oliver, you've said you want to actually *read* that passage aloud, that Gissing wrote it to be shouted. So do it — and then tell me: is Gissing cheering her on, or is the slight excess of it, as you put it, his way of keeping his distance?
questions.intent: Get the passage spoken aloud for radio energy, then use Trevelyan's own ambivalence to open the question of whether Mary's militancy is endorsed or ironized — Leigh and Rosen have completely opposite answers

questions.question: Edmund, I want to give you the last word on something before we move on, because I think it's the real fault line here. You've argued the novel is about the spiritual cost of pursuing absolute independence — that the whole project of self-determination Gissing shows us is a kind of poison. Daniel thinks the novel is showing us that the system is working exactly as designed, and these characters' ideas — however brilliant — are basically adjustments within it. Can both of those things be true at once? Or do they actually cancel each other out?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between the moral-individualist and structural-systemic readings, and see if either expert is willing to concede common ground or dig in harder

steering_notes: The sharpest energy in this segment lives in the three-way tension between Leigh's spiritual reading, Rosen's structural reading, and Trevelyan's performative reading of the same passages — especially c2:p118 and c14:p111. All three experts have staked out different territory on Everard, so that's a reliable flashpoint. Let Trevelyan read aloud when he wants to — it'll change the register of the conversation and give the others something concrete to respond to rather than paraphrase. Watch for Leigh and Rosen talking past each other (moral failing vs systemic design) and step in to force the direct question: are these compatible readings or genuinely opposed? Don't let the segment become a referendum on whether Gissing was a feminist — keep it anchored in what specific lines are actually *doing*.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh reads Virginia's Trafalgar Square moment as grace and renewal; Rosen reads it as managed relief that keeps her compliant — this is the most direct contradiction in the pre-interviews and should be surfaced early

Rosen argues Everard's free union rhetoric leaves material conditions untouched; Leigh argues it reveals a moral deficiency in the man himself — these are not the same critique and pressing both experts to distinguish them could be very productive

Trevelyan's claim that Mary is 'arguing herself into her own convictions' sits interestingly between Leigh (who sees ideological abstraction as spiritually dangerous) and Rosen (who sees it as the only rational response to the system) — Trevelyan's framing might actually be the one both others could partially accept
All three experts want to quote 'rarest of boons' but for completely different reasons — this is an ideal moment to have all three give their reading of the same four words in sequence

segment_name: The Margins of Respectability: Rhoda Nunn and the Cost of Independence

questions.question: Daniel, you've called Fanny Wheatley the novel's 'true protagonist' in this segment — but she barely speaks. Gissing gives us that devastating passage, the wrinkles, the hollow cheeks, the indelible weariness — c12:p83 — and then what? She gets married and we're apparently meant to feel okay about that. Is Gissing exposing the system or is he actually doing the system's work for it by packaging seventeen years of erasure as a kind of redemption?
questions.intent: Get Daniel's sharpest structural reading on the table immediately — that Fanny is the cost, not the sentiment — and open the door for Edmund and Oliver to push back on whether 'the system' is really the right frame

questions.question: Edmund, I want to stay with that same passage — c12:p83 — because you read it very differently. You said this is where Gissing 'breaks your heart through seeing,' not through argument. But Daniel's just told us it's evidence of a political crime. Can a sentence do both things at once? Or does calling it political actually flatten what Gissing achieves there?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Edmund's tragic-humanist reading and Daniel's structural one — get Edmund to defend the idea that aesthetic seeing is itself a moral act, not a retreat from politics

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started that everyone in this novel is trapped by scripts they're either following or trying to escape — and I keep thinking about that line you wanted to read, c14:p141, where Rhoda can't even name what she feels about Everard: 'it was not love, nor the beginning of love; she judged it something less possible to avow.' That's a woman whose whole identity is built on clarity and self-knowledge, and she can't find the word. Is that Gissing undercutting Rhoda, or is it actually the most honest thing he does for her?
questions.intent: Bring Oliver's voice-and-character reading into the centre — get him to articulate what Rhoda's opacity reveals about her, and set up Edmund's agreement and Daniel's counter that this opacity is ideologically produced

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued Monica's so-called weakness is structural — that she was deliberately undereducated and then handed two impossible options. But Oliver was just saying Rhoda is equally trapped, equally unable to name her own desire. If both women are scripted by forces outside themselves, what exactly is Rhoda's education project offering? Is it liberation or just a better class of cage?
questions.intent: Push Daniel to defend or complicate his reading of Rhoda's radicalism — is she genuinely progressive or is her project, as Oliver suspects, its own form of fantasy? Draw out the tension between structural critique and the charge that Rhoda mistakes her need for universal truth

questions.question: Edmund, I want to give you the last word on this before we move on — because you said something in our conversation that's been nagging at me. You said Gissing doesn't believe in solutions, and that's what makes him a great novelist rather than a propagandist. But Daniel would say that's exactly the problem: the novel sees the crime clearly and then calls it tragedy instead of calling it a crime. Is there a difference? And does it matter?
questions.intent: Close the segment with Edmund's biggest claim — that tragedy is the novel's moral achievement, not its evasion — and leave space for Daniel to land one final structural challenge; aim for genuine unresolved tension rather than a tidy conclusion

steering_notes: The segment should feel like it builds — start with the concrete (Fanny's body, the passage) and end with the abstract (what kind of novel is this and what is it asking of us). Don't let the conversation settle into Edmund vs Daniel as a binary: Oliver's formalist and comic instincts are the wild card that keeps both of them honest. If Daniel goes too structural too fast, redirect through Oliver. If Edmund gets elegiac, get Oliver to read something aloud — the Monica declaration, the Rhoda passage — and let the prose do the work. The question of whether Gissing is brave enough to make Fanny's sacrifice a political fact rather than a sentimental one should hang over the whole segment unresolved.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund reads Widdowson's passion (c11:p35) as genuine love rendered without contempt; Daniel reads it as class anxiety and compensatory emotional intensity — if Widdowson comes up, push both of them on whether those readings are actually incompatible or whether Gissing is doing both simultaneously

Oliver and Daniel are on a collision course over Rhoda's education vision (c10:p28): Oliver hears rigidity and fantasy in it, Daniel hears genuine radicalism undermined by its own structural blind spots — get them to read the passage together and disagree about the same sentences

The Fanny passage (c12:p83) is wanted by all three experts and each reads it differently — Edmund as moral seeing, Oliver as prose rhythm and unbearable sadness, Daniel as political evidence. This is the segment's richest cross-engagement opportunity: ask all three to say what the *same sentence* is doing and let the disagreement surface naturally

Monica's declaration 'I can't go their way' (wanted by Oliver and Daniel both) is a pressure point: Oliver hears a childlike desperation that's also 'absolutely wrong about what she's choosing'; Daniel hears structural impossibility, not personal failure. Edmund will likely defend Monica's desire as irreducibly human. All three positions are in genuine tension here

segment_name: Trapped by the Wedding Ring: Monica's Fall and Widdowson's Obsession

questions.question: Daniel, you've said that line about Widdowson's jealous temper — 'if ever a man declared in his countenance the worst species of jealous temper' — sounds like character psychology but is actually describing the marriage contract itself. That's a provocative reading. Can you unpack that? Because on the surface Gissing is just describing a bloke's face.
questions.intent: Get Daniel to open the structural/legal argument clearly so Oliver and Edmund can push back from their character-focused positions

questions.question: Oliver, you'd push back on that, wouldn't you? You called that same passage 'pure acting direction masquerading as narration' — you're reading Gissing as a dramatist watching a man's face, not a sociologist describing a system. Can you read it for us and make the case?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to quote c14:p130 aloud and articulate the theatrical/character reading as a direct counter to Daniel's systemic one — sets up a clean disagreement

questions.question: Edmund, you've got a third position here that I want to push on — you think *both* of them are slightly missing the point. You're saying Widdowson isn't a social symptom and he's not just a theatrical grotesque — he's a man with a corrupted soul. Is Gissing writing tragedy or is he writing a case study?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's moral-psychological reading and force the three-way distinction between systemic, theatrical, and spiritual interpretations into the open

questions.question: Oliver, there's a passage I want you to read — Monica at c15:p135, the moment she realizes she's facing 'no companionship but her husband's.' You called it Monica discovering her own tragedy in real time. But Daniel would say she's discovering the trap was always there. And Edmund would say she's discovering the cost of her own dishonesty. Who's right — or is the passage doing all three things at once?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c15:p135 aloud and then let all three experts fight over what it actually means — the best single passage to crystallize the segment's disagreement

questions.question: Edmund, I have to ask you about Rhoda's asceticism speech at c6:p126 — 'a widespread revolt against sexual instinct.' You read that as Gissing's irony, Daniel reads it as Gissing showing how feminist doctrine accidentally serves the system, and Oliver thinks the whole debate is secondary to Monica's silence. Is Rhoda the most dangerous character in this novel, or is she just the most deluded?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest disagreement of the segment — all three experts have strong, incompatible views on Rhoda's asceticism speech, and this question lets them collide directly

steering_notes: The three experts form a genuinely interesting triangle: Daniel reads everything structurally, Oliver reads everything theatrically and through performance, Edmund reads everything as moral-psychological character study. The goal is to keep all three positions live simultaneously rather than letting any one dominate. Push back when anyone starts abstracting — bring them back to the face, the room, the passage. The Monica silence at c15:p135 is the emotional centre; get it read aloud. The Widdowson smile at c14:p130 is the intellectual flashpoint. Don't let Rhoda's asceticism speech swallow the whole segment — it's a tool, not the destination. Watch for Oliver and Edmund to quietly agree that Gissing is skeptical of ideology, which might strand Daniel; if that happens, push Daniel to respond directly.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel says the Widdowson jealousy passage describes 'the marriage contract itself' — Oliver explicitly calls it 'acting direction masquerading as narration.' These are direct contradictions about what kind of writing Gissing is doing, not just what the passage means. Make them address each other's framing.

Edmund thinks Monica's entrapment is partly self-inflicted through her own dishonesty; Daniel thinks her deception is forced on her by the coercive structure of the marriage. The c15:p135 passage is where this disagreement is sharpest — get them to argue over it using the text.

Oliver and Edmund share a suspicion of ideology-first readings, but for different reasons — Oliver because he thinks silence and performance beat doctrine, Edmund because he thinks conscience beats both doctrine and system. They're allies against Daniel but will diverge on Rhoda, which is worth exploiting.

Daniel's framing of Rhoda's asceticism as 'complicit with patriarchy' directly contradicts Edmund's reading of it as tragic irony about principle replacing humanity. Both are anti-Rhoda but for opposite structural reasons — this is good radio.

segment_name: What Gissing Gets Right (and Wrong): Class, Gender, and the Comedy of Misunderstanding

questions.question: Oliver, you've described Everard as a 'comic grotesque' — basically a man drunk on his own arguments. But I want to push on that, because when he delivers the 'pis aller' speech in c10:p63, a lot of readers find it genuinely melancholy, even honest. Are you saying Gissing is mocking him there, or is the joke something more uncomfortable — like, the speech is both ridiculous *and* true?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to commit hard to the satirical reading and open the door for Edmund to push back with the tragic/moral reading — sets up the central disagreement of the segment

questions.question: Edmund, you said Monica's laugh in c16:p160 is a moral hinge — that she's choosing her own chains. But Daniel, I think, would say she's doing something much colder and more rational: she's calculating what survival requires. So Edmund, is Monica a tragic figure who *fails*, or is she someone who sees the situation with absolute clarity and makes a terrible but logical choice?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to distinguish between moral failure and rational adaptation — creates direct collision with Daniel's structural reading and Oliver's tactical intelligence reading

questions.question: Daniel, let's get specific about Everard's big moment — c18:p17, 'Now there's a woman! Look at her, Mary.' You said his passion is real but it's passion for a specific kind of subordination. Oliver thinks it's pure theatrical self-delusion. Edmund thinks it's the one moment Everard briefly touches genuine virtue. Which is it — and does it actually matter, given what you've said about individual quality being irrelevant to how the system works?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to reconcile his structural reading with a specific character moment — also surfaces the three-way disagreement about what Everard's declaration *means*, which is the sharpest cross-engagement in this segment

questions.question: Oliver, you called Mrs. Luke in c15:p127 the novel's secret weapon — she arrives and basically refuses to let anyone wallow. Daniel seems to think she's exposing the social machinery, Edmund seems to think she's irrelevant to the moral drama. But you're saying she's doing something almost directorial — like she's the only character who can see how absurd everyone else is being. Is she Gissing's proxy? His way of breaking the fourth wall without breaking it?
questions.intent: Draw out Oliver's most playful and distinctive reading, get the others to weigh in on whether Gissing uses comedy structurally or whether it's just local color

questions.question: Edmund, here's the tension I can't resolve: you're saying the novel is essentially conservative — people fail because of moral cowardice, not because the system is rigged. But Daniel would say Rhoda is right about everything and it doesn't save her. Aren't those the same story told from different angles? Or is there a genuine disagreement about what Gissing thinks *could* have saved these women, if anything?
questions.intent: Close the segment by surfacing the deepest philosophical disagreement — whether the novel diagnoses a curable disease (moral failure) or an incurable one (structural oppression) — and force both Edmund and Daniel to say what they actually believe Gissing believed

steering_notes: The segment has a natural three-way tension worth protecting: Oliver's comic/satirical reading, Edmund's moral/tragic reading, and Daniel's structural/class reading. Don't let any two of them gang up on the third too early — the most productive radio comes from keeping all three frameworks in play simultaneously. The three key passages — c10:p63 (pis aller), c16:p160 (Monica's laugh), c18:p17 (Now there's a woman) — should each get at least one moment of direct quotation. If the conversation goes long on Everard, redirect to Monica and Rhoda, where the real disagreements about female agency live. Watch for Edmund and Oliver to find unexpected common ground on Monica's laugh — they read it very differently but both think it's the novel's pivot, and that convergence is worth pausing on.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver reads Monica's laugh (c16:p160) as tactical intelligence and survival; Edmund reads the same gesture as moral evasion and self-destruction — this is the sharpest direct contradiction in the segment and should be surfaced explicitly

Daniel argues Rhoda's intelligence becomes a form of precarity; Edmund argues Rhoda is the moral centre who alone refuses the comfortable lie — they're using her as opposite proof texts for opposite arguments
Oliver insists Everard's pis aller speech (c10:p63) sounds fatuous when read aloud; Edmund thinks it's Gissing at his most penetrating — ask them both to read it and explain what they're hearing

Daniel and Oliver both want to quote 'Now there's a woman' (c18:p17) but for completely different reasons — Daniel to show passion-as-subordination, Oliver to show theatrical self-delusion — letting both explain why they chose the same passage will produce genuine fireworks

segment_name: The Narrator's Irony: How Gissing Unsettles His Own World

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started recording that this novel is basically a dark comedy about self-deception — that these characters aren't wrong, they're *performing*. But I want to test that. When Gissing writes 'Never had it occurred to Widdowson that a wife remains an individual' — is the narrator laughing at Widdowson, pitying him, or something more uncomfortable than either?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to articulate his 'performance not ideology' thesis early, and establish the tonal question that will drive the whole segment — which opens the door for Daniel to push back hard on whether 'comedy' is the right frame for structural violence

questions.question: Daniel, you'd push back on that pretty sharply, right? Because your reading of the Barfoot passage — 'the letter of two lines and an enclosed cheque would as likely as not plunge her into depths' — is that this isn't just Barfoot deceiving himself, it's the narrator catching a whole *system* in the act. Is Gissing's irony a scalpel or a comedy routine?
questions.intent: Force the Oliver vs Daniel disagreement into the open — Oliver sees a novelist of self-deception, Daniel sees structural critique. Get Daniel to argue that calling it 'comedy' actually lets the men off the hook

questions.question: Edmund, I have to bring you in here because you've staked out what feels like the loneliest position in this argument — you're saying the irony cuts *inward*, not outward. That Widdowson isn't a symptom of a system, he's just a man who can't imagine his wife as a separate person. Doesn't that let the institution off the hook entirely?
questions.intent: Put Edmund on the defensive in a productive way — his 'moral failure of imagination' reading is genuinely interesting but vulnerable to the charge of depoliticizing the novel. Let Daniel and Oliver both want to respond

questions.question: Oliver, walk us through the Rhoda letter-burning scene — passage c21 — because you described it as something you can *hear* happening, this ceremonial pacing. But you also said it's not triumph, it's erasure. Daniel thinks it's deliberate disentanglement, purposeful. Edmund hears classical resignation. Who's right about what Rhoda is actually doing in that room?
questions.intent: Use the specific passage to crystallize the three-way disagreement about Rhoda's interiority and Gissing's sympathies — force all three experts to commit to a reading of the same moment

questions.question: Last one, and I want everyone to take a swing at it. The ring scene, chapter 25 — Everard produces a ring despite everything he's argued against marriage. Oliver says it's farce, a man unconsciously performing what he consciously rejected. Daniel, you said the narrator's phrase 'perilous symbol' is Gissing telling us the gesture is still an act of imposition. Edmund reads it as Rhoda seeing through Everard clearly. Can all three of those be true simultaneously — or does one reading have to win?
questions.intent: Bring the segment to a head by asking whether Gissing's irony is finally stable or genuinely undecidable — this should produce either a rare moment of convergence or a satisfying three-way disagreement about what the novel is ultimately doing

steering_notes: The productive tension in this segment runs between Oliver's tonal reading (dark comedy, performance, the narrator's delight) and Daniel's structural reading (ideology, mechanism, diagnosis). Edmund is the wild card who refuses both frames and keeps pulling the conversation back to individual moral psychology. Don't let the segment become a binary Oliver-vs-Daniel debate — keep bringing Edmund back in, because his 'loneliest position' is often the most interesting radio. The Widdowson passage is common ground for all three, so use it early to establish the shared text before the readings diverge. Save the ring scene for last — it's the passage where the disagreements are sharpest and most personal, and it gives the segment a natural climax.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver calls the ring scene 'comedy' and 'unconscious performance' — Daniel calls it 'imposition' — these are not just different tones but different claims about Everard's agency and Gissing's intent. Push them to argue this directly rather than past each other.

Daniel reads Rhoda's letter-burning as preparatory and purposeful; Edmund reads it as resignation; Oliver reads it as control that doubles as erasure. The same passage, three incompatible emotional registers — make them account for the discrepancy.

Edmund's insistence that 'the novel's deepest sympathy is reserved for the paralysis of thought that afflicts all characters' directly contradicts Daniel's claim that Gissing's sympathies lie with the women's refusal. This is a clean, arguable disagreement that should be surfaced explicitly.

segment_name: The Marriage Plot and Its Discontents: Realism Against Romance

questions.question: Oliver, you want us to *hear* this novel — you said you have to read it aloud to understand it. So let's start there. You mentioned the sentence from chapter 26 — 'The incredulity she could not help must either part them for ever, or be to her an occasion of new triumph' — and you said it *breaks* in the middle. What did you mean by that? What does the sentence actually sound like when it falls apart?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the passage and articulate his core claim about prose rhythm as emotional revelation — sets up the disagreement with Edmund and Daniel who read the same sentence completely differently

questions.question: Edmund, you want to quote the exact same sentence — same passage, chapter 26 — but you hear something completely different in it. Oliver hears a performance trap, Daniel's going to tell us it's the system closing in. You're calling it a spiritual crisis, a moral paralysis that's Rhoda's own doing. Make the case. Why is this *her* failure and not society's, or Gissing's irony?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to defend his moral reading against Oliver's stylistic one and Daniel's structural one — the disagreement is sharpest here and this is the segment's central tension

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to Marseilles — chapter 18. Everard's at this gorgeous café on the Cannebière, everything blazing with electric light, and he's writing to Rhoda. Oliver thinks the sentence is secretly funny — Gissing mocking romantic sincerity. Edmund thinks Everard's being weak, self-indulgent. You think he's doing something more sinister. What's actually happening in that letter?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to make his 'colonialism applied to gender' argument in plain language — and provoke Oliver to defend the comedy reading and Edmund to defend the weakness reading

questions.question: Oliver, I want to push on something. You said Rhoda *becomes* the role — that she commits to 'marriage means disgrace' like an actress and then gets trapped by the performance. But Edmund would say the trap is moral, Daniel would say it's economic. Is there actually a difference? Like — does it matter *why* she's trapped if she can't get out either way?
questions.intent: Force Oliver to either defend the distinction between performance-trap and moral/material trap, or concede ground to Edmund and Daniel — creates a triangular argument about what kind of novel this actually is

questions.question: Edmund, last one — and I want everyone to weigh in on this. You said Gissing shows us feminism as a *symptom*, not a solution. Daniel's going to say that's basically blaming the women for being trapped. Oliver might say you're both missing that Gissing finds this *funny* as well as tragic. So which is it — is *The Odd Women* a tragedy of individual souls, a structural indictment of marriage, or is Gissing secretly laughing at all of them?
questions.intent: Final synthesis question designed to produce a three-way disagreement about genre and authorial stance — no right answer, maximum friction, good radio ending

steering_notes: The three readers are using the same three passages to make completely incompatible arguments — that's the engine of this segment. Keep pulling them back to the actual sentences rather than letting them go abstract. Oliver needs prompting to perform or at least read closely; Edmund goes philosophical fast and needs to be grounded in character specifics; Daniel will make the structural argument fluently but may need pushing toward the affective texture of the prose. The Marseilles letter and the chapter 26 sentence are the two live wires — any time the conversation drifts, return to one of them. Don't let 'tragedy' go uncontested — it's doing different work for each of them.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver and Edmund are directly opposed on the chapter 26 sentence: Oliver hears comedy and prose fracture, Edmund hears spiritual annihilation — they should be in the same conversation about that line as early as possible

Daniel's claim that sentiment 'obscures extraction' is a direct challenge to Edmund's entire moral framework — Edmund should be invited to respond to that specific formulation, not just the general materialist reading
Oliver's 'performance trap' and Daniel's 'structural trap' may actually be compatible readings — worth surfacing whether they've been arguing past each other, which could itself be good radio

Edmund's reading of Mary's rejection of Everard (ch 8) as personal moral judgment vs Daniel's reading of it as rationalizing economic interest is a sharp local disagreement that could anchor the middle of the segment if the abstract debate needs grounding

segment_name: Gissing's Unresolved World: What The Odd Women Demands of Its Readers

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started recording that this novel refuses to let readers off the hook — that the 'unresolved' quality isn't a flaw, it's the whole point. But I want to push on that. When Mary speaks in c13:p118, Gissing sets up the anonymous clerk's letter first — we feel his desperation before her certainty arrives. Is Gissing genuinely unsettling Mary's position there, or is he just giving her a more dramatic entrance?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to articulate his 'gap between rhetoric and truth' argument, and draw out the idea that Mary's confidence is performed — theatrical — setting up Edmund's more damning read of her moral confusion

questions.question: Edmund, you've got a fairly devastating take on Mary — you said she's mistaken the removal of obstacles for the achievement of virtue. There's that line in c13:p124, 'Let the world perish in tumult rather than things go on in this way' — and you told me before we started that she doesn't actually mean it. That she's never had to face the tumult. Can you make that case? Because I think Oliver and Daniel are both going to want to fight you on it.
questions.intent: Provoke Edmund into his strongest moral-collapse argument about Mary, which will directly antagonise Daniel's structural reading and Oliver's rhetoric-vs-sincerity distinction — three-way tension in one move

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund is essentially saying everyone in this novel — Mary included — lacks the interior discipline to handle freedom. You're saying something quite different: that it's not about individual character at all, it's the system. So when Widdowson's hand closes with that 'murderous convulsion' in c24:p43 — is that a moral failure or is it, as you put it to me, just a fact? Because those feel like very different novels.
questions.intent: Force the Edmund-vs-Daniel disagreement into the open on the violence passage — Edmund reads it as spiritual desolation, Daniel reads it as structural logic. Get both to commit to their readings and show the stakes of the difference

questions.question: Oliver, you said Gissing's language around Everard and Rhoda in c14:p89 — 'challenge to his manhood,' 'desirable' — is doing something colder than romantic complexity. That desire here is ego, not connection. Daniel is nodding. But doesn't that reading actually support Edmund's point? If nobody in this novel is capable of genuine connection, are we in a structural tragedy or a spiritual one — and does the novel actually know the difference?
questions.intent: Use Oliver as a bridge to force the structural-vs-moral question to a head — his reading of Everard's desire is the point where Daniel and Edmund's positions most productively collide, and Oliver is the right person to name that collision

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you to have a go at this. Edmund, you said the novel's real question is whether any of these characters has the self-knowledge to live well. Oliver says the ending is a deliberate refusal to answer. Daniel says the ending is the answer — the answer is just bleak. What does this novel actually demand of its readers? Are we supposed to choose a side, sit with the discomfort, or has Gissing written something that makes choosing impossible?
questions.intent: Final synthesis question — let each expert give their defining statement about what the novel asks of readers. Should produce three genuinely different answers and a satisfying close to the segment

steering_notes: The natural fault line in this segment is Edmund's moral-individual reading versus Daniel's structural-systemic reading, with Oliver positioned as the most aesthetically focused of the three — he cares about how Gissing does it, not just what Gissing means. Use Oliver to translate between the other two when the argument gets abstract. The clerk's letter in c13:p118 is a good early anchor because all three experts have strong but different takes on it. Push for actual passage readings aloud — Oliver especially wants to perform the violence sentence from c24:p43, let him. Watch for Edmund retreating into abstraction about 'moral wisdom'; bring him back to the text. Daniel can tend toward the theoretical too — if he starts talking about 'patriarchal architecture' without quoting anything, redirect him to c14:p89 and Everard's specific language.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that Mary 'doesn't mean' the tumult line (c13:p124) directly contradicts Daniel's reading that she's sincere but structurally insulated — this is a productive distinction worth naming on air

Oliver's argument that the novel is 'skeptical of rhetoric' sits uncomfortably between Edmund (who thinks Mary is morally confused) and Daniel (who thinks she's politically naive but not dishonest) — Oliver's framing could either unite or inflame both of them

All three experts want to quote the murderous convulsion sentence from c24:p43 but for completely different reasons — Edmund: spiritual desolation; Daniel: structural logic; Oliver: the prose itself enacting violence. Worth flagging this as a moment of triangulation

Daniel's point that intellectual equality 'just makes women more interesting to men' as conquest is a direct challenge to any reading of Rhoda as successfully resistant — Edmund will agree for different reasons, Oliver will resist
